intro: Every category sells a little differently. A serum buyer wants to see texture, a sneaker buyer checks the sole, and a coffee buyer wants to watch the pour. These pages sort ideas by what you sell, so you can start with the shots that answer your shoppers' real questions instead of guessing. Each one covers the photos and short videos worth making first, the details to get right in your upload, and questions other sellers in that category often ask.

Start on the page for your main product, even if your catalog spans several categories. The examples there are matched to how people shop for that item: close texture shots for beauty, fit and fabric shots for clothing, scale and setting shots for home goods. You can open the photo or video tool from each example and reuse the same product photo across every look.

faq.q: Which industry page should I use for a mixed or unlisted catalog?
faq.a: Start with the page that matches your main product, then borrow a scene from another category when it fits. Pet supplies, toys, stationery, and outdoor gear can use the same photo and video tools.

faq.q: Can I use a phone photo to get started?
faq.a: Yes. Use a sharp, evenly lit phone photo with the whole product in frame; professional equipment is not required. Upload only a photo you own or have permission to use.

faq.q: What's the difference between the industry pages and the templates?
faq.a: Industry pages help you choose the buyer detail to show; templates apply a chosen look to the photo you upload. Plan the shot on an industry page, then open a linked template to produce it.

faq.q: Can one product photo be used for both photos and videos?
faq.a: Yes. A clear square photo with the whole product visible can produce white background and lifestyle photos, and it can also guide vertical video scenes. Keep the original uncropped so each format has room to reframe.

faq.q: Do the industry pages cover which ad format works for each platform?
faq.a: Yes. Open the linked platform page for the format used on TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube Shorts, Amazon, or Shopify. The platform page explains the slot and the file shape to choose.

faq.q: Will the result keep my product shape and color?
faq.a: It keeps the shape and color more reliably when your full product is visible in the source photo. Compare the downloaded result with the item you sell before publishing.

faq.q: Which ad moment should I make first for a new product?
faq.a: Start with the moment that answers the buyer’s first question: texture for beauty, fit for clothing and shoes, scale for jewelry and home goods, setup for electronics, routine for wellness, or taste and serving for food.

faq.q: Can I use the photos and videos from these pages in paid ads?
faq.a: Yes. Downloaded files are watermark-free and licensed for commercial use, including paid ads, listings, and social posts. Keep any claims, prices, and added text accurate and follow each platform’s ad review rules.

steps_h2: How to Make AI Product Content by Industry in 3 Simple Steps
steps_lead: Start with one product photo, choose the buyer moment for your category, and download an asset you can post.

steps.d: Open the page for your category and add one photo of the item. The examples show what should stay visible in that upload.
Choose a matched moment, such as a demo, try-on, pour, or unboxing. Run one photo through several scenes to cover more buyer questions.
Review the result and save it. Add exact wording in your editor, then publish it to your listing, feed, or paid ad.

directory_scenes.d: Show an adult applying a small amount and holding the package beside the finished texture for a clear routine moment.
Show the garment on a person in motion so shoppers can judge fit, fabric and the finished look.
Hold the shoe up on the trail and point to the outsole lugs so buyers see the grip before the first step.
Use hands to open the package, lift one piece and hold it close enough to show scale and finish.
Show the gadget being set up and used for one task, with the controls visible in the same frame.
Place the product in a real morning or gym-bag routine without implying a health outcome you cannot support.
Show an adult serving the drink or snack, then taking the first sip or bite so the serving context is clear.
Show the starting clutter or mess, then the product in use during one simple organizing or cleaning step.
